newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sterling skids after Labour wins by-election.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sterling skids after Labour wins by-election.

text.p: Sterling skidded around one pfennig in a knee-jerk reaction to a landslide by-election win for the opposition Labour party which pushed the ruling Conservatives into a Parliamentary minority.
While the Labour win at Wirral South was expected, sterling was queasy as the 18 percent swing to Labour was bigger than expected as was the voter turnout, at just over 70 percent.
"There is no doubt that the turnout and the swing were on the high side of expectations," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International.
Analysts, however, said any downwards move for the pound would be temporary as currency markets had already factored in a Labour victory.

"The effect of the by-election should not have a large impact because the unpopularity of the current government is hardly a surprise," said Klaus Baader, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell

Sterling dipped a pfennig, initially, to a session low of 2.7345 marks against 2.7470 in late Europe on Thursday before recovering some steam and trading at 2.7440 marks, nearly unchanged from late Europe, around 1100 GMT.

Against the dollar, sterling slid just over a cent to session lows of $1.6168 as European markets digested the Labour win, but by midmorning the pound had clawed back some of its early losses and was trading at $1.6283/93.
"I wouldn't expect the by-election to have a prolonged effect because it (the result)," has not come as that much of a surprise," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW.
Currency jitters could have been compounded on Friday had there been any chance of Labour forcing the Conservative government to call a general election, expected in May, sooner, said analysts.
But that is unlikely after the Ulster Unionists made it clear that they will back the Conservative government if Labour calls a vote of no confidence.

John Prescott, the deputy leader of Britain's Labour party, said it would be very difficult to unseat the Conservative government even though it was now a minority after losing the Wirral South by-election. "We can harass and harry them. What we can't complete is a confidence motion if the other political parties don't join us," he told BBC radio.
Prescott, though, said Labour would not simply sit back and wait for May 1, which many believe will be the most likely date of the next election.
With the South Wirral by-election over, some analysts are concerned that Labour's landslide could be mirrored in the coming general election.
"We didn't expect them (Conservatives) to get thrashed that much. If that is repeated in the general election, it's going to be pretty one-sided," said David Coleman, chief economist CIBC Wood Gundy.

Some economists have said Labour landslide could give the party, out of government since 1979, a mandate to be tougher on economic policy and have even raised the possibility of it reneging on pre-election commitments.
IBJ's Hannah said while everyone is already on election watch and Labour seems set to win the general election, a landslide at the polls would be unsettling for markets.
"That is a risk scenario," said IBJ's Hannah. "Markets might feel uncomfortable with that. With a huge (Labour) majority, there is a risk that a party may engage in more radical policies."
Any threat to the currency, however, will be short-lived as markets now see little difference between the two parties.
"The currency markets have come to the view that the prospect of a Labour government doesn't hold too much disruption," said Robin Aspell, chief economist at National Australia Bank.
Wood Gundy's Coleman said things, however, could change after the general election when Labour gets a chance to show they have really changed.

"In terms of fiscal policy the big question is how will they square the circle of the higher spending they have promised, in some quarters, with Mr Brown's desire to be known as the Iron Chancellor," said Coleman.

While some analysts said the outcome at Wirral could have been an excuse to take profits on sterling's solid run this week, the market should also be clearly relieved at the result as it allays fears of a hung parliament at the general election.
"Probably the worst scenario for markets, no clear majority for either party, would appear to have only a marginal probability at the next general election," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Baader.
